previous.passage: Not the river, Omar, Aponi said, before I had even opened my mouth. We were standing on the stone bridge below the mesa in the spring of 1879, the first time I had seen her since my family moved east to the trading post. As children we had crossed this bridge daily; the summer before I left, her brother had been caught by the flood beneath it. We had never spoken of it, and now we kept a fence of silence around that one field, walking beside it with great care. So we talked of horses, of my father's ledgers, of the new schoolhouse. Whenever the water grew loud below us, she pointed to a hawk or asked about the weather in the east. I let her. At dusk the shadows of the arches stretched across the dry wash, and a flock of sheep came down the far slope.

previous.passage: Although the salt-water pool at the community center in Dayton, Ohio, had been Paloma's for thirty years, she let me open it that morning, handing me the ring of keys with a ceremony that made me laugh. I was nineteen, her apprentice lifeguard, and restless; the new aquatic park across town had offered me a job at twice the pay. I joked about it while we tested the water and skimmed the leaves. Paloma joked back, asking whether the new place came with a wave machine and a manager half my age. Then she stopped skimming. She told me the pool had been dug by her father's crew, that she had taught every child in the neighborhood to float in its shallow end, and that she had hoped someone would know where the drain stuck in winter. I put down the net. Across the water, the morning light lay flat and bright on the tiles.

previous.passage: Hasan, our foreman, had a habit of counting chairs. At every wedding we staffed in Thessaloniki that summer of 1872, he walked the hall twice before the guests arrived, tapping each chair back and muttering numbers, and I, newly hired, trailed behind him trying not to smile. That evening the hall was so crowded that the count fell apart at once; guests perched on window ledges, and the musicians spilled onto the stairs. I expected an outburst. Instead Hasan stood still among the dancers, and something in his face loosened. He told me, quite softly, that his father had been a foreman too and had once been dismissed because a single guest went without a seat. Then he handed me his tally slate. Keep it or break it, Sadia, he said. Beyond the doors, a cart rolled past on the wet stones.

previous.passage: Four things lived in Jomo's back room: a treadle machine, a dressmaker's dummy with no head, a radio that caught only one station, and the runner-up plate from the 1979 district chess final, which he had lost and I had won. I was twelve then. Afterward, everyone said I had been brilliant to beat a grown man, and I had believed them for ten years. Now I sat on his cutting table while he hemmed a pair of trousers, and I asked, idly, why he kept the plate behind the radio instead of on the shelf. He did not answer at once. __He pinned the hem, then unpinned it, then pinned it again in exactly the same place.__ At last he said that my father had been ill that winter, and that he had wanted me to have something to be proud of that was not about my father. "You played well," he said. "I played worse on purpose." The radio announced the noon news, and a bus ground its gears in the street below.

previous.passage: How long can a person avoid the woman who saw her cry on a crowded bus? For you, Nadeesha, the answer was eleven days. You took rickshaws to the ceramics studio instead, though they cost more than your clay. You told yourself Kamala, who had driven the number 6 for as long as you had ridden it, would have forgotten how you sobbed over a cracked bowl in your lap while the whole bus watched. Then, on the twelfth day, Kamala walked into the studio. She had signed up for the beginners' class. She sat at the wheel beside yours and made, with great concentration, a lopsided cup that collapsed. She laughed, loudly, at herself. You laughed too, and the room laughed with you, and the shame you had been carrying shrank to something that fit in a pocket. Not that you will admit this. You still claim the rickshaws were for the fresh air. Kamala's cup, refired, now holds your brushes.

previous.passage: "Ma'am, this was in the type case," said the boy who brings the paper stock, and he held out my husband's brass composing stick, which I had searched for since the funeral. I confess I was short with him. I believed, as widows are inclined to believe, that every hand in the press room of Port of Spain was waiting to carry off some piece of my husband's trade. previous.passage: Nova had come up the mountain road above Marrakesh to repay an old loan, and the snow trapped both of them in Dalia's cabin for three days. On the first morning, Nova counted the money twice and set it on the table, but Dalia only pushed it aside and asked for help clearing the woodpile. Under the drift, the wind had uncovered a tin box Dalia had buried years earlier, holding every receipt from the loan, each one marked forgiven in faded pencil. Nova had spent a decade dreading this visit, rehearsing apologies on long bus rides. Now Dalia simply fed the stove and asked about Nova's work, as if no account had ever been open. Outside, the snow kept sliding off the cedar branches in soft, heavy sheets that hissed as they struck the ground.
